titleEn: Shallow-Water Dive Drowning - Cardiac Arrest With a Suspected Cervical Injury

patient.name: Owen Patel
patient.affectEn: unresponsive teenager lying on his back on soft sand, wet, in swim shorts, cyanotic, foam at the mouth, no movement and no response to pain; after ROSC he coughs and gags, breathes weakly on his own (about 6 a minute) and stays deeply unresponsive (GCS 6, later 8)
patient.speechEn: none - he cannot speak at any point in the call; the history comes from his friends, the lifeguards and his mother

scene.settingEn: Main beach at Cultus Lake near Chilliwack, 1520 hrs on the August long weekend. Sunny, air 28 degrees C, water 19 degrees C. Crowded public beach, hot sun, soft sand. The patient is on the sand about 5 metres from the waterline. Chilliwack General Hospital is 20 minutes away.
hazardsEn: large crowd (about forty people) pressing in close, several filming
hot, soft sand - poor footing, and compressions on sand are ineffective

bystanders.knowsEn: Started compressions on the sand as soon as the friends pulled him out - about a minute before you were dispatched. Will keep doing compressions, swap with you, carry equipment or help lift on your direction. Saw nothing before the friends pulled him out.

He ran off the end of the dock and dove in head-first into water they estimate at about one metre deep, roughly 15 minutes before your arrival (about 1505). He did not resurface. They thought he was joking for about a minute, then pulled him out face down and unresponsive after about three minutes in the water. No alcohol or drugs that they know of - they hesitate when asked, then say: "Not that we know of."

Being brought over by a friend; arrives during the resuscitation, distraught. He is healthy and plays soccer; no recent illness. Asthma diagnosed at age 8 - blue inhaler used maybe twice a year, no recent flare, nothing taken today that she knows of. No daily medications. Allergic to shellfish - his face swells. He ate a hot dog and a slushie about an hour ago. No previous head injury, no seizures, no known heart problem, no fainting, no family history of sudden death. She will consent to anything that helps him and needs someone to stay with her.
Arriving as you do. Will move the crowd back, stop the filming and stay with the mother when asked.
Arrive with you carrying the AED. Will apply the pads, take over compressions, hold manual stabilization of the head, fetch the scoop or backboard and help lift - only on your direction.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: AED (fire first responders) with adult and pediatric pads
BVM with oxygen tubing, oxygen kit
hard collars, head blocks / foam rollers and straps
scoop stretcher and backboard (hard spinal immobilization devices)
BP cuff and stethoscope, pulse oximeter, glucometer, thermometer, penlight
PCP only: supraglottic airway, IV start kit, PEEP valve / CPAP

dispatchEn: 1520 hrs, August long weekend. Code 3 to the main beach at Cultus Lake near Chilliwack. A 16-year-old male dove head-first from a dock into shallow water, did not resurface, and was pulled out by friends after roughly three minutes. Bystander CPR is in progress. Air temperature 28 degrees C, water temperature 19 degrees C, sunny. Fire first responders arrive with you and have an AED. Chilliwack General Hospital is 20 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch adds: bystanders say he went in head-first off a dock into about one metre of water and they saw him floating face down. Two lifeguards started compressions on the sand about one minute ago. A large crowd has gathered and police are two minutes out.
arrivalEn: Crowded public beach in hot sun. You walk across soft sand toward a tight ring of about forty people; several are filming on their phones. A teenage boy lies on his back on the sand about 5 metres from the water, wet, in swim shorts. Two lifeguards are doing chest compressions on him; the sand gives under him with every push. Fire first responders arrive with you and have the AED in hand. Police are pulling up behind you. A friend is bringing his mother over. One patient.
firstLookEn: A teenage boy lying on his back on soft sand, wet, cyanotic, not moving, with foam at his mouth. Two lifeguards are doing CPR on him; the sand compresses under him with each compression. A large crowd is pressing in and several people are filming.

primary.locEn: Unresponsive: no movement, no response to voice and no response to a painful stimulus. (AVPU = U.)
primary.airwayEn: Water and frothy vomit in the mouth and airway - suction is needed (adult suction time 10 to 15 seconds). There is no gag reflex, so an OPA is tolerated once inserted. Once suctioned, opened with a jaw thrust and an OPA is in, the airway stays clear.
primary.breathingEn: DURING THE ARREST: apneic - no breathing (checked together with the carotid pulse, no more than 10 seconds). With BVM ventilations and a good seal, the chest rises. AFTER ROSC: respirations 6 per minute, agonal and inadequate - they must be assisted with the BVM at 10-12 per minute.
primary.circulationEn: DURING THE ARREST: NO carotid pulse on a 10-second check. No external bleeding. Every pulse check before the engine announces signs of life finds NO pulse; a pulse check during the arrest is the circulation assessment, not a vital sign. AED (give the device prompt only when the candidate turns it on and analyzes): first analysis - "No shock advised." AFTER the engine announces signs of life (ROSC): a carotid pulse of 118, weak and regular. Any analysis after ROSC - "No shock advised."
primary.rbsEn: Rapid body survey once the resuscitation is running: a 4 cm abrasion and swelling over the forehead and the bridge of the nose, consistent with striking the bottom; no other injury, no bleeding; chest and abdomen unremarkable; pelvis stable. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: cyanotic, cool and wet. (Examiner note, never volunteer: a head-first dive into about one metre of water is a high-risk cervical mechanism - manual in-line stabilization throughout, but never at the cost of delaying compressions.)

history.ccEn: (The patient cannot speak.) (Lifeguard:) "He dove off the dock and didn't come up. His friends pulled him out and he wasn't breathing, so we started CPR."

opqrst.oEn: (Friends:) "He ran off the end of the dock and dove in head-first. It's only about a metre deep there. That was about 15 minutes ago."
opqrst.sEn: (No pain score is possible - he is unresponsive.)
opqrst.tEn: (Friends:) "He didn't come back up. We thought he was joking around for about a minute, then we pulled him out - face down, not moving. He was in the water about three minutes." (Lifeguard:) "We started compressions on the sand straight away."

history.painScoreEn: Cannot be obtained - he is unresponsive (GCS 6 after ROSC, 8 later); it does not become obtainable during this call.

sample.sEn: (Cannot be obtained from the patient.) (Friends:) "He was fine before he dove in."
sample.aEn: (Mother:) "He's allergic to shellfish - his face swells up."
sample.mEn: (Mother:) "Just his blue puffer for asthma, and he hardly ever uses it - maybe twice a year. Nothing today that I know of. No daily medications."
sample.pEn: (Mother:) "He's healthy. He has asthma - since he was 8 - but he hardly ever needs his inhaler. Nothing else."
sample.lEn: (Mother:) "He had a hot dog and a slushie about an hour ago."
sample.eEn: (Friends:) "He ran off the end of the dock and dove in head-first. It's only about a metre deep there." (Only if asked about alcohol or drugs - they hesitate:) "Not that we know of."

fe.generalEn: (Mother:) "He's healthy - he plays soccer. He hasn't been sick."
fe.respiratoryEn: (Mother:) "Asthma since he was 8. He uses the blue inhaler maybe twice a year. No recent flare-up."
fe.cardiovascularEn: (Mother:) "No heart problems that we know of. He's never fainted. (Only if asked:) Nobody in the family has died suddenly."

findings.headNeckEn: 4 cm abrasion over the forehead with swelling over the bridge of the nose, no depression, no blood from the ears. (Collar in place once applied.)
findings.chestLungsEn: Equal air entry with coarse crackles at both bases. No rib injury, no chest wall deformity.
findings.abdomenEn: Distended with swallowed water and air; soft.
findings.backEn: Checked during the transfer onto the device: no deformity, no tenderness elicited.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: No injury. Sensation and motor function cannot be assessed in an unresponsive patient - document CSM as unassessable, not normal. Radial pulses present after ROSC.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: No injury. Sensation and motor function cannot be assessed (unresponsive). Pedal pulses present bilaterally after ROSC.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: immediately post-ROSC - the first set; no vital signs exist during the arrest (CPR and the AED come first)

resp.character: agonal; being assisted with the BVM at 10-12 per minute

vitalsSets.skin: cyanotic improving to pale; cool and wet
vitalsSets.spo2: 84% rising to 95% with the BVM and 15 L oxygen

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: en route, about 7 minutes after set 1, with assisted ventilation and warming; GCS and pupils improving

resp.character: some spontaneous effort; assisted with the BVM at 10 per minute

vitalsSets.skin: pale and cool, no longer cyanotic
vitalsSets.spo2: 97% on the BVM with 15 L oxygen

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: As the 2-minute cycle ends he coughs, gags and starts weak breathing on his own.
He coughs, gags and starts weak breathing on his own.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge and plan for a resuscitation with a spinal problem: AED, BVM and oxygen, suction, airway adjuncts, collar, scoop, towels and blankets, all carried to the patient in one trip
Decide the priority before you arrive: in cardiac arrest, resuscitation comes first and spinal precautions are maintained by hand during it - the two are done together, not one after the other
triggers: CPR with c-spine held by hand
don't delay CPR for the collar

expected.actionEn: Verbalize hazards (crowd, filming bystanders, water, hot sand, your own footing), environment, MOI (head-first dive into approximately one metre of water, roughly three minutes submerged) and people (one patient, lifeguards, family)
triggers: mechanism is a dive into shallow water

expected.actionEn: Don gloves and eye protection; ask police to move the crowd back and to manage the people filming, and get the patient onto a hard surface such as a backboard or the scoop because compressions on soft sand are ineffective
First look: teenage male, cyanotic, wet, unresponsive, with foam at the mouth and CPR in progress on an unstable surface
Assess LOC / AVPU: unresponsive

Maintain manual in-line stabilization by a second rescuer throughout the resuscitation - a head-first dive into shallow water is a high-risk cervical mechanism, but this is done by hand and never at the cost of delaying compressions
Open the airway with a JAW THRUST, not a head-tilt chin-lift, suction the water and vomit for no more than 10 to 15 seconds, and insert an OPA once you confirm there is no gag reflex
Confirm apnea and ventilate with a BVM and high-flow oxygen with a good seal; do not attempt to drain water from the lungs and do not perform abdominal thrusts
Confirm pulselessness on a 10 second carotid check and start high-quality compressions at 100-120 per minute, 5 to 6 cm deep, ratio 30:2, with full recoil and interruptions under 5 seconds
Move him onto a hard surface for effective compressions - compressions on soft sand are ineffective, and the transfer doubles as the spinal packaging
Rapid body survey once the resuscitation is running: identify the forehead abrasion as evidence of striking the bottom, and rule out other injury
Note the skin as cyanotic, cool and wet
High-flow oxygen attached to the BVM during arrest and maintained after ROSC, targeting SpO2 at or above 94% without hyperventilating
Remove the wet swim shorts, dry him and cover him with blankets - even on a hot day a wet patient loses heat fast, and after ROSC he stays supine on the spinal device rather than sitting up
triggers: keep him supine on the board

expected.actionEn: Categorize as RTC and keep that category after ROSC
Ready to load within 15 minutes with full spinal packaging completed during the resuscitation rather than after it
Use lifeguards, fire and police effectively: compressions, equipment, crowd control and family support, while you keep the airway and the resuscitation running
Establish the chief complaint: cardiac arrest following a shallow-water head-first dive and submersion

HxC/C from bystanders covering the drowning specifics: water depth, head-first entry, submersion time, time to first compressions, what was done by bystanders, water temperature, and any alcohol or drug use
triggers: did he go in head first

expected.actionEn: Pain cannot be scored in an unresponsive patient - document that and re-attempt as the LOC improves
Past medical history from the mother, including the asthma
Medications, including the inhaler and anything taken today
Allergies - shellfish with swelling
Last oral intake - a full stomach an hour before submersion raises the aspiration risk
GCS with all three components, repeated frequently after ROSC
Blood pressure - the first post-ROSC blood pressure is a key number for the receiving team
Pulse rate, rhythm and quality, checked centrally and rechecked frequently in case of re-arrest
Respirations - 6 and agonal is inadequate and must be supported, not just recorded
Skin assessed hands-on
Pupils - size and reaction are the key neurological observation after a hypoxic arrest
SpO2 with the target at or above 94% while avoiding hyperventilation
Blood glucose - mandatory with a decreased LOC
Temperature - a wet patient from 19 degree water is hypothermic even on a hot beach day
FE - General health
FE - CNS
FE - Respiratory (the asthma history matters for both the arrest and the post-ROSC ventilation)
triggers: how often does he use his inhaler

expected.actionEn: FE - Cardiovascular (family history of sudden death would suggest a primary cardiac event rather than a simple drowning)
triggers: sudden cardiac death in the family

expected.actionEn: FE - GI/GU
FE - Integumentary
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT
Head and neck examined before the collar is applied, with the forehead injury documented as evidence of the impact
Chest examined with six-site auscultation; crackles at both bases indicate aspiration
Abdomen examined - gastric distension from swallowed water raises the vomiting and aspiration risk
Back examined during the transfer onto the spinal device
Upper extremities examined, with sensation and motor documented as unassessable in an unresponsive patient
Lower extremities examined with pedal pulses documented
High-quality CPR at adult ratios: 30:2, 100-120 per minute, 5-6 cm deep, full recoil, interruptions under 5 seconds, compressor changed every 2 minutes

Apply the AED with adult pads and follow the asphyxial arrest sequence: with two rescuers, apply the AED during 5 cycles of one-person CPR, then analyze; resume CPR immediately when no shock is advised
Airway management: jaw thrust, suction for no more than 10 to 15 seconds at a time, OPA once there is no gag reflex, and BVM ventilation with high-flow oxygen and a good mask seal
triggers: corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw

expected.actionEn: Maintain manual in-line stabilization throughout the arrest and complete the spinal packaging during the transfer onto the hard device - never delay compressions for a collar
triggers: don't stop compressions for the collar
onto the board as a unit

expected.actionEn: After ROSC assist ventilations at 10-12 per minute targeting SpO2 at or above 94% without hyperventilating, and keep reassessing for re-arrest
Remove wet clothing, dry him and cover him with blankets to manage the 34.8 degree temperature, and keep him supine on the device rather than sitting up because of the arrest and the spinal mechanism
triggers: keep him supine on the device

expected.actionEn: Assign a crew member or police officer to the mother, and delegate crowd control so bystanders are not filming the resuscitation
Reassess ABCs every 2 to 3 minutes post-ROSC and after every move
Manage the vomiting immediately: suction, tip the whole immobilized patient as a unit, and never remove the straps to roll him
triggers: turn the board on its side

expected.actionEn: Keep the AED attached for the whole transport in case of re-arrest
Second full set of vitals within 5-6 minutes for a priority patient, with the improving GCS and pupils reported as a trend
Repeat the temperature and continue passive warming with dry blankets
Notify the receiving hospital immediately on ROSC, including submersion and arrest times
Complete hand-off with the resuscitation timeline, the AED result, the post-ROSC course and the spinal precautions
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes with all resuscitation times recorded

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate turns on the AED / attaches the pads and has it analyze the rhythm (personally or by delegating)

the SECOND AED analysis / rhythm-and-pulse check of this call, done after the further 2 minutes of CPR that followed the first 'no shock advised' analysis. Never record it for the first analysis, and never for pulse checks after signs of life.
candidate verbalizes checking for or seeing chest rise with the BVM ventilations (or another sign that the ventilations are effective)
candidate delays starting or resuming chest compressions in order to apply a collar, head blocks or a board, or to finish spinal packaging first

candidate abandons manual in-line stabilization (no one holding the head before the collar, blocks and straps are on), or rolls, sits up or moves the head freely during the resuscitation or after ROSC. Handing the head over to the partner, fire or a lifeguard is NOT a release.
candidate opens the airway with a head-tilt chin-lift instead of a jaw thrust

candidate tries to drain water from the lungs (e.g. turns him over or lifts his hips to drain water, or does abdominal thrusts). Tipping the whole immobilized device to clear vomit from the mouth is NOT this event.
candidate suctions for longer than 15 seconds at a time
candidate stops compressions for more than about 5 seconds for airway work, the pads, the collar or the transfer (pauses for the AED analysis itself are correct)
candidate keeps the compressions going on the soft sand through the first 2-minute cycle without moving him onto a backboard, scoop or other hard surface
in this asphyxial arrest the first analysis is done without about 2 minutes (5 cycles) of CPR first, or CPR is stopped while the pads are put on
candidate uses pediatric AED pads on this 16-year-old (adult pads are correct past puberty)

AFTER the examiner has described signs of life (coughing, gagging, breathing), the candidate continues or restarts chest compressions in a later line without first checking for a pulse, or continues compressions after a pulse has been found. Never record this for the candidate line that the signs-of-life description was answering.
after ROSC, candidate ventilates clearly faster than 10-12 per minute (e.g. 20 or more a minute, or rapid continuous squeezing of the bag)
after ROSC, candidate stops assisting the ventilations (e.g. takes the BVM off and switches to a non-rebreather) while his own respirations are still 6-10 per minute and inadequate
after ROSC, candidate removes the AED pads, switches the AED off or packs it away
candidate sits him up, puts him in the recovery position off the device, or removes him from the spinal device after ROSC (e.g. because the drowning guideline says to sit patients up)
when he vomits, candidate undoes the straps / takes him off the device to roll him instead of tipping the whole immobilized device as a unit
candidate inserts a supraglottic airway, applies CPAP or PEEP, starts an IV or gives an IV medication. Saying these are outside EMR scope, or that the PCP will do them, is NOT this event.
PCP stops or delays compressions or the AED analysis to insert a supraglottic airway before high-quality CPR and the AED are established

drugs.doseEn: 0.4 mg IM or IV (repeat after 3 minutes per the monograph if SpO2 >= 94% and ventilations > 10 are not achieved), or 4 mg IN. Indication: respiratory depression / depressed mental status secondary to actual or suspected narcotic use - nothing in this history points to opioids (friends know of no drugs; pupils 5 mm, not pinpoint); his arrest is asphyxial from submersion.
Not indicated: indication is bronchospasm / wheeze, and he has crackles from aspiration, not wheeze (adult MDI 4 x 100 mcg; nebulized 5 mg)

trackNotes.emrEn: This entire resuscitation is EMR scope and is graded on the mechanics: high-quality 30:2 adult CPR on a hard surface, adult AED pads with the asphyxial sequence (two rescuers: pads on during 5 cycles of CPR, then analyze), jaw thrust with suction limited to 10-15 seconds and an OPA once there is no gag, BVM with high-flow oxygen and a good seal, manual in-line stabilization from arrival with the collar and device applied without interrupting compressions, and post-ROSC assisted ventilation at 10-12 per minute targeting SpO2 at or above 94%. Wet clothing off, dried and blanketed for a temperature of 34.8, kept supine on the device with suction in hand, and the AED left attached the whole way. CPAP or PEEP, a supraglottic airway, IV access and drugs are beyond EMR scope. No Functional Enquiry.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds the 9-system Functional Enquiry taken from the mother, a supraglottic airway once high-quality CPR and the AED are established, vascular access, and PEEP or CPAP after ROSC if indicated for the aspiration picture. The resuscitation mechanics, the asphyxial AED sequence and the spinal precautions are identical at both levels.

sourcePages: scenario etr-06 (data/practical/emr-trauma-1.json); BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (altered LOC or unconsciousness, cardiac arrest, respiratory arrest), p.11 Primary survey interventions (cervical spine stabilization; airway maintenance and suctioning; ventilating the non-breathing patient; CPR for an absent carotid pulse), p.25 Spinal Management (manual stabilization, hard collar, device, foam blocks, secure the body, do not tape the head), p.29 Hypothermia (remove wet clothing and cover; mild hypothermia > 32 to < 35 C - warm blankets, hot packs, preheat the ambulance), p.37 Drowning / Near Drowning (spinal motion restriction as indicated by the mechanism; position sitting up applies to the conscious patient; remove wet clothing and dry; IPPV if required; resuscitation per the appropriate guideline; PCP: PEEP or CPAP if indicated), p.40 Adult CPR/AED (CPR 30:2, analyze as soon as possible, no shock advised - 2 minutes of CPR then analyze), p.42 CPR/AED basic concepts (interruptions under 5 seconds, change operators every 2 minutes, move the patient early only if CPR cannot be effective where he lies, avoid hyperventilation, SGA for PCPs once high-quality management is established), p.43 Adult CPR/AED basics (100-120 per minute, 5.0-6.0 cm, 30:2, no shock advised - resume CPR immediately), p.44 Asphyxia arrest (drowning: if alone, 5 cycles of CPR before applying the AED; two rescuers - apply the AED during 5 cycles of one-person CPR, then analyze), p.45 Suctioning (10-15 seconds in the adult), p.72 Naloxone, p.77 Salbutamol; EMALB grading criteria timing rules (priority: ready to load within 15 minutes, vitals interval 7-8 / >9 minutes)
